title: Draft: Faster Frame Generation, Sharper Cockpits, and Eleven Languages
summary: Draft for 0.20.0 RC1, pending the build 4 flight. This combines the unreleased 0.19.4 fixes with the Frame Generation speed and image-quality work, hardware optical flow in Dynamic Interpolate, and app, OSD and installer localization. Flight-dependent claims and the lead ceiling default remain marked for confirmation.

items: Less GPU work per real frame. The speed pass reduces the work spent matching motion and preparing generated frames. In replay profiles on an RTX 5090 at 5424x5356 per eye, FG GPU time was about 20% lower, or 0.7-1.2 ms less per real frame, against the pre-speed-pass build. DCS FG at 2x with shader flow measured about 0.6 ms of GPU per real frame in flight.

Dynamic Interpolate can use NVIDIA hardware optical flow. Choosing NVIDIA hardware as the motion source now applies in Dynamic too. A new option under Motion source, Fall back to Shader when hardware flow can't keep up (on by default), switches Interpolate to shader flow when hardware flow repeatedly fails to keep up, then tries hardware again; turn it off to keep hardware flow. GPUs without supported NVIDIA optical flow use shader flow. Dynamic Interpolate on hardware flow held about 90 fps in a 16-minute MSFS flight. The OSD shows the active source. Fallback reasons are recorded in the log and the app's internal status.

Auto gives a lower multiplier a fair trial. A failed step-down probe no longer spends the full normal settle period disrupting the game, and a short burst of late frames during the switch no longer rejects a multiplier the game can sustain. Changes to settings, the runtime clock or output images still get the normal settle.

A lead ceiling for the frame history. When Frame Generation is timing the game so far ahead that newer captures replace images it still needs, the ceiling can bring that lead down. It checks the result and backs out a lowering that repeatedly makes frames late, so it does not impose the same fixed limit on every game.
Lead ceiling default, if approved on: The adaptive lead ceiling is enabled by default.
Lead ceiling default, if approved off: The adaptive lead ceiling is off by default.

Video memory accounting includes cached hardware-flow images. Frame Generation now counts the images it keeps after a motion-quality or view-layout change, so its working-memory report reflects those allocations.

Sharper near detail in games that provide usable depth. Generated frames now use cubic resampling for nearby content by default. MSFS cockpit fine detail in generated frames measured 92-98%, up from 83-88%, in replays. Interpolate also keeps more valid cockpit motion through small movements.

Empty depth is never adopted. A depth image cleared to one value no longer becomes a false near surface that warps the whole view. Menu depth that is simply left clear keeps being checked until the game supplies real scene depth. Near/far corrections and scale changes now need meaningful evidence, and sparse but usable depth can be accepted without treating uniform depth as valid.

More stable depth decisions. Depth contradicted by the other eye is rejected, and a dropped reading must show sustained good evidence before it returns. A usable replacement can take over directly. Filling gaps in resolved depth now runs separately so neighboring GPU threads cannot change one another's result.
Usable depth from one eye can help both eyes. If a game supplies useful depth to only one eye, Frame Generation can use it for the other eye too. Empty depth still stays unused.

Hardware flow keeps flat and black menu areas still. DCS menus could show shifted copies of the menu in the black surround, and the Mission Editor could show ghost tiles on a plain background. Hardware optical flow now keeps those areas still when that matches the image, rather than carrying nearby content across them.

Off now stops the remaining features too. Switching VectorXR Enabled off hides the OSD, stops its bindings, sounds and performance sampling, stops Frame Generation toggles, and disables the remaining head-prediction, Quadviews visualization and focus-sharpening work. Starting a game with it off also leaves the eye-gaze extension alone. If it is switched off during a running session, the session's four-view layout and Frame Generation pacing and graphics bridge remain until the game restarts; generated frames stop immediately.

Eleven languages. The app, tray, OSD and installer support English, Simplified Chinese, Russian, Spanish (Spain), Portuguese (Brazil), German, Japanese, French, Polish, Korean and Traditional Chinese. Choose the app language under Settings; the OSD can follow the app or use its own language. OSD columns also fit the translated labels. The non-English catalogs began as machine translations and welcome native-speaker review. Patch-note content remains in English.

A public status file. Tools can read %LOCALAPPDATA%\VectorXR\api\status.json through a documented, add-only interface, separate from the internal runtime relay. It identifies the game and session and includes Frame Generation state and rates, the game's target rate, measured refreshes per real frame, runtime holding and Auto's step thresholds. See docs/status-api.md.

Targets and cleanup follow the actual session. Targets account for runtimes that hold frames to every second refresh, and fields no longer stay frozen after generation stands down. The file is removed when its owning session ends or its process exits, including abandoned-session cases, while preserving another game's file.

Safer Vulkan shutdown. The graphics bridge waits for the game's final rendering before destroying its images, including releases with no final frame submission and private depth images. If completion cannot be proved, it keeps the backing resources alive instead of freeing them under queued work. It also avoids handing an image back to a game that is already tearing down.
Startup with stacked OpenXR layers. An extension check no longer reaches OpenXR Toolkit through an intervening layer such as OpenKneeboard before an OpenXR instance exists, which could crash startup.

Input reconnect rules survive unusual session endings. Missing input devices resume normal reconnect checks after device work drains at teardown. If a runtime refuses to end a session, the running game keeps the session reconnect rules that avoid periodic hitches.
Repeated capture requests keep working. A capture request being removed by the layer no longer leaves the capture script waiting indefinitely before the next request.

Local build freshness checks. The local signing helper now rejects an outdated source or build definition and mismatched staged manifests or sounds, so it cannot silently accept the wrong layer artifacts.

More useful support logs. Frame Generation summaries include the lead and prediction horizon actually reported to the game. Queue diagnostics and rejected Turbo predictions provide more evidence when investigating pacing problems.

title: Star Citizen Stability, Performance Headroom, and a System Tray
summary: A stability release with a few new tools. Star Citizen's head wobble with Frame Generation is fixed on Virtual Desktop and Pimax, and an unplugged controller no longer stalls games every two seconds. Frame Generation holds steadier over long sessions, works with OpenComposite games that leave frames open, and no longer uses images that failed to allocate when video memory runs low. The On-Screen Display gains a PERFORMANCE row showing CPU and GPU headroom and video memory, and the app gains a system tray icon. Settings carry over from 0.19.2 unchanged.

items: The head wobble is fixed. With Frame Generation enabled for Star Citizen, the world swam against head movement, even with generation toggled off in-game. The game draws each frame after handing its image over, and VectorXR copied the image at the handover, so the headset was shown an older frame with the current head position. It was clearest on Virtual Desktop, where the frame was three frames old, and fainter on Pimax, where it was one. VectorXR now takes the image when the frame is submitted, as a runtime does. Frame Generation's frames come from the same images, so they are fixed too.

An unplugged controller no longer stalls the game every two seconds. If any VectorXR binding pointed at a controller that wasn't connected, VectorXR tried to reach it every two seconds for the whole session, and each try stalled the game's frame. That showed as a regular hitch, and with Frame Generation as extra latency. In a game, VectorXR now looks for a missing controller only when Windows reports one plugged in and when VR starts. Outside a VR session it still retries regularly.
Rescan inputs (Settings > General > Input Devices) makes running games look again, for a controller connected mid-session that VectorXR didn't detect.

Steadier over long sessions. When video memory was close to its limit, Frame Generation could switch between keeping three and five real frames each time it re-engaged, rebuilding all its images each time. It now keeps its choice until memory really runs short, and the log says when it changes.

Recovers from late pauses. Frame Generation retries by itself after a pause, but only three times per session, so a fourth pause late in a long flight stayed paused until you toggled it. The retries now come back after five minutes without a pause.

OpenComposite games no longer pause Frame Generation. OpenVR games running through OpenComposite (Automobilista 2, for example) can leave a frame open and begin another. One such frame left Frame Generation a frame behind for the rest of the session, and it soon paused. It now drops those frames, as the runtime does.

Fewer failures under GPU pressure. A failed image allocation (low video memory) could leave Frame Generation using images that didn't exist; that is fixed. Changing the motion quality while NVIDIA's optical flow hardware is busy now waits for it, and a watchdog releases a match that never finishes.

Layer metadata is kept. Colour scale and bias, and alpha-blend settings a game attaches to its layers, now carry through to generated frames. A game that attaches metadata Frame Generation can't carry over gets Frame Generation off for that session, with the reason on the OSD and in the log, instead of frames that lose it.
Logs and summaries show more for support: the real frames kept, how long Dynamic waits after standing down, retries used, the game's view sizes when they change, and its full depth description.

New PERFORMANCE row (on by default in the expanded layout, optional in compact): how much of the frame budget the game's CPU time and the GPU leave free (headroom), and which one limits you when that is clear, plus the game's video memory use against its budget. It samples only while the row is shown.

The OSD shows in games that restart VR at launch. OpenComposite games (seen with Automobilista 2) start their VR session twice at launch, and on Virtual Desktop the OSD then stayed off, even when its binding showed it, until a setting was saved.

System tray icon. The tray menu has the health status, the VectorXR switch, the log level and Export Debug. Changes made there are saved at once. With the tray On (the default), closing the window keeps the app in the tray, and starting VectorXR again brings the window back. With it Off, closing the window quits. The app and tray only manage your settings: VectorXR works in your games with both closed, as long as VectorXR Enabled is on.
Export Debug is also under Settings > Logging.
Settings saved by 0.19.3 stay readable by 0.19.0-0.19.2 layers, so you can keep an older copy installed.

DCS no longer crashes with OpenXR Toolkit and Quadviews (#108). OpenXR Toolkit supports two views only, and VectorXR usually sits below it, where Toolkit would get DCS's four quad views. In that order VectorXR now keeps Quadviews off, so DCS runs stereo. The log says why, and the OpenXR Layers page shows a warning. Turn OpenXR Toolkit off for DCS, or set it to bypass DCS, to use Quadviews. VectorXR directly above Toolkit no longer crashes at startup either.

Tools can read Frame Generation's live rates (#103). While Frame Generation runs, the runtime status file has its mode, frame rate, multiplier, refresh rate and real, output and distinct frame rates as numbers, for tools such as MSFS_AutoFPS. The fixed rates now read "up to 1/2 the refresh rate", and the guide explains what happens below that rate.

Upside-down images from OpenComposite (#107). When an OpenComposite build flips an image with a negative height, which OpenXR does not allow, Frame Generation pauses with a message naming OpenComposite's invertUsingShaders option. Before, it failed with no explanation.
In helicopters, Interpolate can show artifacts around the rotors and in the sky behind them.
On Varjo headsets with Quadviews, focus sharpening is off in DCS while Frame Generation runs.
Frame Generation does not use Star Citizen's depth yet: the game fills only one eye's depth image.

title: Compatibility, Stability, and Frame Generation Pacing
summary: A broad fix release. VectorXR now loads on PCs without the Visual C++ runtime and can no longer be crashed by an old one a game ships. Frame Generation paces better on Varjo, with overlays such as OpenKneeboard, after hitches, and with runtimes that hold frames to half rate; Interpolate can use NVIDIA's optical flow hardware at fixed frame rates (experimental), and the Quadviews diagnostic visualization works with Frame Generation. Turbo no longer treats normal Star Citizen and MSFS exits as crashes, the On-Screen Display refreshes at the rate you set, and the app protects your settings and layer list better. Settings carry over from 0.19.1 unchanged.

items: VectorXR carries its own C++ runtime. On a PC without the Microsoft Visual C++ redistributable, VR failed to start in every OpenXR game while the Health page said Ready. A game that ships an older runtime could also crash VectorXR at startup. Neither can happen now, and a game's regional number format can no longer change how VectorXR reads its settings.
Windows user names and game folders with non-English characters no longer stop VR from starting.
Games that quit without closing VR (Star Citizen, MSFS 2024) exit cleanly: VectorXR no longer does work at process exit that could hang or crash it.
A runtime that stops answering no longer freezes the game under Turbo. After about two seconds the game carries on, and if the runtime keeps holding frames, Turbo turns itself off for the session.
If VectorXR itself hits a fatal error, it names it in its log and hands it to the game's crash reporting instead of making the game vanish without a trace.

Fewer missed refreshes on Varjo. On Varjo headsets, and with overlays such as OpenKneeboard on any headset, Frame Generation's frames waited for the game's GPU work before they could be shown. With a busy GPU in Dynamic, that dropped about one refresh in ten.

Lower latency in Dynamic. When the runtime skipped a refresh, Frame Generation counted the game's frames as late and timed the game further ahead, up to its maximum, where it stayed. Missed refreshes no longer push the game ahead.

Auto stops stuttering when it cannot step down. Auto tried a lower multiplier on a timer, which cost about two seconds of stutter each time the game could not keep up. It now tries only when the game has room to spare.

Auto under half-rate smoothing. With Pimax Smart Smoothing or similar settings that hold frames to half the refresh rate, Auto climbed to 3x or 4x and slowed the game to about 10 fps. It now passes frames straight through, as Dynamic does, and tries again later.

Shorter delay after a hitch. A hitch raised how far ahead the game is timed, and it came back down only after 20 to 60 seconds; it now returns within about 10 seconds, so the head pose the game renders with stays closer to the moment it is shown (Star Citizen in particular).

Auto no longer gets stuck at 4x. After the runtime's frame timing recovered from a stall, Auto could step up on the moment of re-engaging, and once at 4x it had no way down even when 4x itself slowed the game (Star Citizen on Virtual Desktop fell to about 22 fps). It now settles first, and tries 3x again when 4x keeps running late.

Interpolate can use NVIDIA's optical flow hardware (experimental). At a fixed or Auto frame rate the game is held to every second refresh or more, which leaves the hardware time to measure the motion, so Interpolate now uses it when Motion source: NVIDIA hardware is chosen. On Star Citizen captures it keeps visor text readable and generated frames as sharp as real ones, at about three times the GPU time for motion and up to one refresh more latency. Dynamic still uses Shader. Profiles that already had NVIDIA hardware chosen use it in Interpolate at fixed rates after updating; pick Shader to keep the previous behaviour.

Diagnostic views are easier to spot. The Frame Generation page warns while a diagnostic view is on, and the log names it. Left on, the Confidence view paints generated frames red where they fall back to the real image.
Changing the multiplier or turning Frame Generation off while a game runs no longer leaves Dynamic's old state behind, and the log no longer reports engagements that did not happen.

Frame Generation's summary now shows how far ahead of its display the game renders (and how much that varies), and Debug logs record each layer's space, the game's HUD layer and the views the runtime returns: the data needed to pin down the remaining Star Citizen shake reports.

Normal Star Citizen and MSFS exits no longer block Turbo. These games exit without closing their OpenXR session, so Turbo's crash guard read every normal exit as a crash and kept Turbo off at the next launch. A real crash still blocks it, and the log now says why.
An antivirus scan of one of Turbo's files no longer turns Turbo off for the session or loses its history.
Refreshes at the rate you set. 20 Hz gave about 10 Hz before.
No longer shows old values or the previous layout for a moment after you show it, switch layout or change its settings, and recovers when turned off and on after a drawing failure.
Drawing it costs about a fifth of the CPU it did, and each refresh uploads only the rows the panel uses.
The DEBUG LOG and diagnostic view tag stays up in a compact layout with nothing else selected.
Changing Quadviews Tracking Mode during a session keeps eye tracking working.

The Quadviews diagnostic visualization works with Frame Generation. In DCS with Frame Generation on, Frame Generation now draws the visualization into every frame it shows, real and generated, instead of it being unavailable.
Emulated quad views give the focus views a visibility mask that hides nothing, and the log records how the eye-tracked inset moves (for reports of streaks around the inset on SteamVR).
OpenKneeboard's swapchains no longer make the quadviews compositor rebuild its outputs.
Varjo focus sharpening no longer rebuilds its target every frame after a failure, and stays current after a slow frame.
When a game never asked for quad views, the log says so instead of suggesting a restart.

Your settings are safer. Clearing a number field and saving no longer turns every module off. If settings.json cannot be read, the app shows the real error and Save no longer overwrites the file with defaults.

OpenXR Layers page: machine-wide changes no longer report the previous request's result, moving a layer no longer rewrites other vendors' entries, and Home and Health report the VectorXR registration that actually loads and refuse to enable a second copy.
Cancelling an uninstall no longer leaves VectorXR unregistered.
Export Debug now includes the Frame Generation trace, keeps the start of long logs, and writes a compressed ZIP.
The app stays responsive during joystick scans, UAC prompts and sound previews, and a joystick HAT that reports centered as 0xFFFF is no longer read as up-left.
Log Retention above 7 now keeps that many logs.
In helicopters, Interpolate can show artifacts around the rotors and in the sky behind them.
On Varjo headsets with Quadviews, focus sharpening is off in DCS while Frame Generation runs.

title: Frame Generation Fixes for Varjo, SteamVR, and Slow Games
summary: Fixes Frame Generation's Dynamic mode on Varjo headsets, a periodic stutter on SteamVR, and generated frames dropping out in slow games that hitch. The On-Screen Display now shows when debug logging or a Frame Generation diagnostic view is on. Settings carry over from 0.19.0 unchanged.

items: Dynamic works on Varjo headsets. After a game paused its frames, as DCS does while loading a mission, Varjo's runtime reported frame times far in the future for up to a minute. Dynamic could engage meanwhile and show old frames instead of generated ones, and stopping could freeze the game for about two seconds. Frame Generation now waits for the runtime's frame timing to recover before it engages, and the On-Screen Display and the app read Waiting for the runtime's frame timing to recover meanwhile. Stopping never holds the game for more than a moment.

Steadier when the runtime briefly drops to half rate. Varjo's runtime holds frames to every second refresh for a few frames after a late one. Frame Generation no longer lets that push the game's frames further ahead, which added latency and repeated frames.

No more periodic stutter on SteamVR under heavy load. When SteamVR missed a refresh, Frame Generation briefly took the game's pace to be half the refresh rate, pushed the next frame several refreshes ahead, and bunched the ones after it: a small stutter every fraction of a second, worst with a busy GPU (low flying, heavy graphics mods). It now keeps the game timed to the refresh rate.

Slow games that hitch keep their generated frames. Each hitch made Frame Generation time the game a refresh further ahead, and it did not come back down before the next one. In a game running near 30 fps, such as Star Citizen, the game soon ran further ahead than the frames Frame Generation keeps, refreshes repeated old frames, and Dynamic eventually stood by. Hitches now add at most one refresh, and it comes back off between them.

Diagnostic settings show in the header. An amber tag after the VectorXR name reads DEBUG LOG while debug logging is on, and TINT VIEW, FLOW VIEW, or CONFIDENCE VIEW while a Frame Generation diagnostic view colors generated frames. Left on, the tint view looks like flicker, and debug logging costs some performance. The On-Screen Display preview in the app shows the same tag.
On Varjo headsets with eye-tracked foveation, debug logs show whether the game submits the focus views' field of view as the runtime located it.
In helicopters, Interpolate can show artifacts around the rotors and in the sky behind them. Reports with Export Debug attached are welcome.
On Varjo headsets with Quadviews, focus sharpening is off in DCS while Frame Generation runs (as in 0.19.0).

title: Experimental Frame Generation, Plus Pivot and Turbo Upgrades
summary: Adds experimental Frame Generation: VectorXR fills the refreshes a game misses with generated frames, so your headset gets a fresh image every refresh even when the game can't keep up, in Direct3D 11, Direct3D 12, and Vulkan games. Also lets Pivot's Enhanced Motion keep working inside Snap Views, adds Position Assist and soft deadzones, keeps games running when the runtime rejects a Turbo frame, and makes Quadviews eye tracking more dependable.

items: Using VectorXR in online games with anti-cheat, including Star Citizen, is at your own risk, and that includes your game account. Official releases are code-signed, and VectorXR has run under Star Citizen's Easy Anti-Cheat in testing, but no game developer has endorsed it, and a developer can change what its anti-cheat allows at any time.
Report problems with VectorXR, Frame Generation included, to VectorXR rather than to the game's developer.

A new Frame Generation page adds generated frames between a game's frames, so the headset gets a fresh image every refresh even when the game renders fewer. It works in Direct3D 11, Direct3D 12, and Vulkan games, in stereo or with Quadviews.

It stays off until you turn it on for a game: add a profile for the game on the Frame Generation page, save, and restart the game. Turning it off applies at once. The page's Setup guide walks through the steps.

Dynamic (the default) lets the game run as fast as it can and fills the refreshes it misses; it stands by while the game holds the refresh rate on its own. Fixed holds the game at 1/2, 1/3, or 1/4 of the refresh rate (2x, 3x, 4x) or chooses among them (Auto).

Interpolate (the default) has the fewest artifacts and shows everything about one game frame later; it measures motion on the GPU's shader cores. Extrapolate adds no latency and shows more edge artifacts; on NVIDIA RTX 20-50 GPUs it can measure motion with the GPU's optical flow hardware (Motion source: NVIDIA hardware), which it needs to look its best.
In Direct3D 12 games that send depth to the headset, such as MSFS 2024 with Motion reprojection: Depth, generated frames use it, so cockpit instruments and text stay still as your head moves.
Advanced settings tune flow quality, artifact suppression, and the motion limit.

The On-Screen Display shows FG ON and the frames per second the headset gets beside its FPS (or FG STBY, FG WAIT, FG PAUSED, FG OFF, FG N/A), a Frame Generation row in the expanded layout, and an optional status line in the compact one.

The Frame Generation page lists running games with their live status. Diagnostic view can tint generated frames or overlay motion and confidence, and an optional A/B toggle binding switches generated frames off and on in game.

Turn off runtime smoothing (SteamVR Motion Smoothing, Pimax Smart Smoothing, Virtual Desktop SSW, Meta ASW) for games that use Frame Generation, and keep the runtime at full refresh. Check both the runtime and the headset's own software: SteamVR showing Motion Smoothing as Not Supported says nothing about Pimax Play's settings, for example. If the runtime still holds Frame Generation's frames to half rate, the On-Screen Display's expanded layout reads Runtime holds frames to half rate: check its smoothing, the log names the settings that can do this, and Dynamic holds off until the runtime gives every refresh again.
Get the game to at least half the headset's refresh rate on its own first, for example 45 fps at 90 Hz. Frame Generation fills the gap from there; below it, artifacts grow quickly.
Turbo stays off in sessions where Frame Generation runs and reads Paused for Frame Generation; your Turbo profiles are not changed.

So far tested on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 with a Pimax Crystal Super on PiOpenXR and SteamVR, in DCS (Direct3D 11 with Quadviews), MSFS 2024 (Direct3D 12), and Star Citizen (Vulkan). AMD and Intel GPUs are untested: the Shader motion source works on any GPU, but the bridges that carry Direct3D 11 and Vulkan games to Frame Generation have not been verified on AMD.

It needs video memory for the real frames it keeps (three to five, about 6 bytes per pixel per eye each) and for its output images: about 3 to 4 GB in all at 6864x6908 per eye (about 4 to 5 GB for Direct3D 11 and Vulkan games, whose bridge keeps a shared copy of the game's images), and under 1 GB at 3000x3000. The log reports what it uses.

Known limits: it does not use game motion vectors or mask HUDs yet, so text, HUDs, and gauges can shimmer on generated frames, and fast motion and newly revealed areas can warp, more so with Extrapolate.

On SteamVR with Pimax's own SteamVR driver, the On-Screen Display can lag behind head turns or show a double image while Frame Generation runs. Hide it with its binding (Ctrl+Alt+F10 by default) if it gets in the way.

In DCS with Quadviews, the Quadviews diagnostic visualization is unavailable while Frame Generation is on for the game, because Frame Generation composes the quad views itself. Turn Frame Generation off for the game and restart the game to use the visualization.
When you report a problem, say whether Frame Generation was on, and attach Export Debug from Home.

New Apply Enhanced Motion to Snap Views: a motion profile can keep its rotation assistance and Position Assist working around a selected Snap View for the same application. Motion profiles without it keep Snap Views exclusive, as before.

New Position Assist adds sideways lean, height, and forward/back movement as you turn, with start and full-offset angles, Gentle and Strong starting points, and optional per-direction tuning. It stays level and follows the snapped view.
New Deadzone Transition eases sensitivity in beyond the deadzone instead of switching at its edge, for all directions or each direction separately.
Instant (0 s) Snap View and nudge transitions apply on the next frame, keeping both eyes and tracked controllers in step.

Snap View profiles no longer take part in activation or Always Active, and a control shared by an activation, a Snap View, and a nudge triggers only one of them. Only the profile that owns the nudges, the selected Snap View or the engaged motion profile, responds to nudge input.
The OSD shows Snap View state on a second Pivot line when the application has Snap Views.

Runtime frame errors no longer stop the game: Turbo re-establishes the frame on the game's own frame thread and continues with Sequenced pacing for the session. Recovered faults appear in the Turbo Safety fault log and do not block Turbo.
Async pacing on runtimes that reject early frame calls, such as Windows Mixed Reality, now waits for a late runtime frame instead of dropping it with an error.
Ending a VR session, quitting the game, or a game resizing its render targets can no longer hang on a pending Turbo frame.

The On-Screen Display, Depth, Depth Lock, Turbo, Turbo metrics capture, and Frame Generation toggles each take several bindings, one for each device you fly with, so swapping a HOTAS for a HOSAS keeps them working. Any one of a toggle's bindings acts.

Eye tracking works alongside games that set up their own eye-tracking bindings, recovers after the headset loses and regains focus, and keeps working when a game recreates its VR session. The log now explains why gaze is unavailable when it is.
Focus Resolution goes up to 300% and both resolutions adjust in 1% steps. Above 200% the app explains the extra GPU memory and compositing cost.
In DCS with Quadviews, the On-Screen Display is now its own layer, as in every other game. On Pimax headsets its edges can now show the same slight color fringing as in other games.

With Log Level: Debug, a flight recorder keeps recent frame-call history and freezes snapshots of stalls, faults, and recoveries, and, with Frame Generation on, of Dynamic stand-downs and runtime halving, so problems that appear after a long session can be reported with Export Debug.
Export Debug keeps every session's main log ahead of older recorder history.

Each session's log names the graphics card, its driver version and video memory, and the OpenXR runtime in a Session graphics line, with a second line for the Direct3D 12 device Frame Generation uses in Direct3D 11 and Vulkan games.

Earlier versions of VectorXR can't read the settings this version saves, even with Frame Generation off, and turn every enhancement off when they meet them. Export your settings before upgrading; to go back, follow the steps in this release's notes on GitHub.

title: In-Headset OSD, Sharper Pivot Views, and Turbo Timing Controls
summary: Adds a customizable in-headset performance display, fixes Pivot's eye-tracked foveation alignment in MSFS 2024, introduces per-profile Turbo timing strategies, and makes Turbo and controller bindings more dependable.

items: New On-Screen Display page adds an optional head-following panel showing application FPS, frame times, a frame-time graph, Turbo state, Pivot, and active enhancements.
Works in Direct3D 11, Direct3D 12, and Vulkan games, including Quadviews sessions.
Choose a detailed or compact layout, arrange its rows, and set placement, size, opacity, accent color, and a 12- or 24-hour clock. Save your favorite layouts as presets.
Position the panel with a live desktop preview, or pop the preview out into its own window while you adjust settings.
Press Ctrl+Alt+F10 to show or hide it and Ctrl+Alt+F11 to switch layouts. Both shortcuts can be reassigned to keyboard, joystick, or hat inputs.
Known issue: on Pimax headsets, the panel's edges can show slight color fringing, except in DCS with Quadviews.
Fixes the high-resolution region drifting away from your gaze when Pivot turns the view in MSFS 2024 with eye-tracked foveated rendering.
Physical leaning now follows the rotated view, including combined yaw and pitch, and Snap View transitions pass smoothly through 180 degrees.
Keeps your seated position correct after you reset or recenter your view in SteamVR, Oculus, or Pimax.

Adds Toolkit-style and Custom timing strategies to custom profiles, with advanced prediction and frame-cap controls for experimentation. Performance Diagnostics labels each capture with the strategy it used.
Switching Turbo off in game keeps frames in order, avoiding the errors and freezes some Async setups hit at that moment.
When Turbo Safety stops Turbo, or Turbo is disabled while a game is running, frame pacing settles immediately instead of stuttering until the game restarts.
Shows restart requirements and the active timing choice more clearly in the desktop app and OSD.
Pausing a Turbo performance capture now saves everything captured so far.
Connects joysticks and HOTAS devices in the background, removing periodic frame-time spikes when a bound device is missing or reconnecting.
A switch that is already on when its device connects no longer toggles Turbo, Pivot, or the OSD by itself.
The OpenXR Layers page recognizes when VectorXR is running as administrator and applies machine-wide layer changes without an extra permission prompt.
Adds collapsible setup guides to the Depth and Quadviews pages and clearer descriptions across the enhancement pages.

title: Turbo Safety, Eye Tracking Correction, and Better Diagnostics
summary: Introduces Turbo Safety, improves automatic pacing and diagnostics, adds Quadviews eye-tracking correction, and welcomes the DienerTech Discord community.

items: Introduces Turbo Safety to protect against interrupted sessions and repeated runtime faults. Review faults, retry blocked setups, or clear history from one page. Protection is on by default and can be disabled globally or per custom profile.
Improves frame prediction timing and recovery from pacing failures. Use the in-game Turbo toggle to retry after a safety stop.
Auto now tests Async first, tries Sequenced when needed, and remembers a strategy after 60 seconds of stable play.
Opens Turbo testing to DCS with SteamVR and synthesized Quadviews. Results still depend on your headset and runtime setup.
Adds optional Flip Z Only eye-tracking correction for setups where the focus region moves backwards. Leave it on Default if tracking already works correctly.
Shows submitted peripheral and focus resolutions in the Dimensions tooltip while a Quadviews game is running.
Keeps useful Turbo performance comparisons visible after a brief game relaunch.
Expands debug exports with fuller logs, Turbo performance and safety data, settings, and runtime diagnostics for easier troubleshooting.
Keeps startup health checks responsive while layer signatures are checked in the background.
The DienerTech Discord is live! Join the community to share setups, compare results, and follow VectorXR news.
Introduces Community & Announcements on Home, with access to Discord and Ko-fi support.
Prevents duplicate VectorXR layers from loading when installing alongside a development build.

title: Smoother Turbo and More Reliable Pivot
summary: Makes Turbo more dependable in DCS, keeps Pivot movement stable in complex rendering situations, improves Quadviews diagnostics and controller reconnects, and adds a headset test utility for validating future fixes.

items: Fixes a rare freeze that could occur when a game began preparing its next frame unusually early.
Keeps timing consistent when games request extra frame updates and recovers safely when a frame cannot be submitted.
Adds broader automated testing for Turbo startup, steady play, failure recovery, and compatibility fallbacks.
Keeps the same Pivot adjustment throughout each displayed frame, even when a game checks headset tracking more than once.
Corrects Pivot in games that prepare tracking and the final image through different rendering paths, preventing movement from being applied from the wrong point of reference.
Handles unusual rendering layouts more cautiously, preferring an unchanged view over a potentially incorrect Pivot adjustment.
Keeps Quadviews focus and gaze guides aligned with the image actually being displayed, even when a game prepares frames ahead of time.
Slows repeated checks for unavailable HOTAS and joystick devices instead of retrying every frame, while allowing their bindings to recover automatically when the device returns.
Condenses repeated input failures into concise reconnect updates instead of flooding the log.
Adds an optional visual test app that exercises Pivot and Turbo directly on a real headset without requiring a particular sim, aircraft, or mission.
Includes several Pivot movement scenarios and a Turbo stress test designed to expose timing problems that are difficult to reproduce during normal play.
Creates a repeatable way to confirm changes across different headsets and headset software, helping future fixes arrive with stronger real-hardware validation.

title: Signed Windows Releases
summary: Adds verified DienerTech code signatures to VectorXR's Windows application, OpenXR layer, and installer.

items: Signs the VectorXR configuration application and OpenXR API layer DLL as DienerTech LLC using Azure Artifact Signing.
Signs the final NSIS installer after it contains the signed application and layer payload.
Applies RFC 3161 timestamps so Windows can continue validating each signature after its short-lived signing certificate rotates.
Uses passwordless GitHub workload identity federation, keeping private signing keys and reusable Azure credentials out of the repository.
Restricts signing authority to the VectorXR certificate profile and release environment.
Verifies every Authenticode signature before generating checksums or publishing release assets, and rejects release tags outside the master branch history.

title: Snap Views, Nudges, and Quadviews Diagnostics
summary: Adds accessible Pivot view modes and reusable controls, a guided Quadviews diagnostic overlay, faster binding workflows, polished configuration pages, and safer upgrades.

items: Adds a profile-level choice between Enhanced Motion and Snap Views, so each application can use natural motion amplification or binding-selected fixed poses.
Introduces unlimited named Snap Views with yaw, pitch, smooth transitions, optional origin-relative position offsets, and independent Hold or Toggle bindings.
Includes a four-view preset for Look Left, Look Right, High 12, and Check Six while preserving 1:1 natural head tracking around every selected pose.
Adds reusable yaw and pitch Nudge Sets with configurable step sizes, transition time, directional bindings, and a Center Nudge Offset action.
Lets profiles share one Nudge Set or copy it for independent controls, with an explicit option to keep nudges available while Pivot is inactive.
Hardens Pivot pose caching and view-return transitions to prevent bounce and keep Snap Views, nudges, and Enhanced Motion composed predictably.
Adds an in-headset visualization for peripheral and focus regions, blend boundaries, head center, configured offset, raw gaze, filtered gaze, and tracking availability.
Adds live Show or Hide control from the Quadviews page during an active synthesized D3D11 session, plus an optional in-headset toggle binding.
Includes an interactive overlay guide that maps visible symptoms to focus, tracking, smoothing, deadzone, and transition settings.
Makes joystick discovery less disruptive by sharing scans, pausing discovery during capture, and listening only to the selected device.
Adds manual button and HAT-direction assignment alongside targeted input capture.
Refines Pivot profile cards, subpages, summaries, controls, dropdowns, and dark-mode styling for the expanded configuration workflow.
Preserves existing 0.15 and 0.15.1 profiles, bindings, module settings, and unknown configuration fields while adding the new 0.16 defaults.
Creates a one-time backup of the pre-0.16 settings document before the first save or reset, so the previous configuration remains recoverable.
Corrects the generated configuration schema for new Pivot and binding fields and expands migration, schema, runtime relay, and Pivot behavior coverage.

title: Eye Tracking Compatibility Fix
summary: Fixes OpenXR action-set attachment handling that could leave Quadviews eye tracking inactive in DCS.

items: Restores Quadviews eye tracking when DCS is used with additional OpenXR API layers, including hand-tracked cockpit controls.

title: Pivot Controls and Stepped Motion
summary: Pivot gains flexible multi-binding activation and independent stepped-motion tuning, while Quadviews receives safer session behavior and clearer setup guidance.

items: Assign multiple keyboard, joystick, or HOTAS inputs to Pivot activation, Set Origin, and Release Origin without duplicating profiles.
Choose Toggle or Hold behavior per activation binding. Always On profiles can use those same bindings to suspend and resume Pivot while keeping automatic engagement as the baseline.
Moves Set Origin and Release Origin into a dedicated Origin Controls workflow with clearer summaries and binding-conflict guidance.
Migrates existing Pivot activation and origin bindings to the new model while preserving their previous runtime behavior.
Separates Stepped yaw and pitch tuning, with independent deadzone, trigger, amount, hysteresis, and maximum-extra controls.
Extends Advanced Axes to Stepped mode so yaw left, yaw right, pitch up, and pitch down can each use their own response.
Replaces stepped smoothing with explicit Instant and Glide transitions. Glide uses a bounded duration, continues smoothly when another step is triggered, and settles without overshoot.
Preserves legacy stepped settings through migration and keeps Continuous and Stepped directional tuning independent.
Defers Quadviews enable or disable changes until the active OpenXR application exits, avoiding mid-session compositor startup and teardown.
Marks settings that need a game restart for their complete effect and distinguishes them from controls that update live.
Clarifies the supported quad-view workflow, recommended DCS setup, provider conflicts, focus and peripheral resolution, and the experimental compatibility scope.
Warns when an enabled custom profile has no assigned applications and therefore cannot activate.
Improves Pivot summaries, advanced tuning layouts, Depth guidance, Quadviews labels, and the usage documentation and screenshots.
Adds stage-specific DirectInput diagnostics for device creation, acquisition, polling, and state-read failures, including retry results.
Hardens runtime capability detection when a lower OpenXR layer returns an incomplete or structurally unreliable extension list.
Expands automated coverage for configuration migration, multi-binding activation, stepped glide behavior, runtime capability policy, and Quadviews session activation.

title: Introducing Depth Lock
summary: Depth Lock gives you direct control over how virtual-world geometry is rendered and submitted, pairing tuned stereo depth and convergence with headset-native OpenXR geometry through a new visual workflow.

items: Depth Lock formalizes render/submission geometry pairing as a first-class VectorXR feature: tune the virtual world's stereo geometry, then submit with the headset-native eye poses and field of view.
The new live Depth Pairing Map makes that relationship visible, showing how Stereo Depth and Convergence combine across all four nearer/farther and flatter/stronger outcomes.
Configure Depth Lock per application and control it in-headset with a dedicated binding and activation/deactivation sounds.
Rebuilds the Depth interface around World Scale, Stereo Depth, and the Convergence Plane, with directional labels, net-effect guidance, override warnings, and a guided tuning sequence.
Uses comfort-oriented +/-25% Stereo Depth and +/-5 Convergence ranges by default, with explicit extended-range controls for +/-100% and +/-25.
Preserves matching decimal precision across Stereo Depth and Convergence controls.

Tracks tuned render geometry separately for each projection layer's reference space, view configuration, and view count so Depth Lock restores the correct native geometry in layered OpenXR applications.
Preserves unrelated composition layers while reporting the exact layer topology VectorXR forwards downstream.
Reduces synthesized D3D11 Quadviews memory pressure by rendering directly into compatible runtime output textures, while retaining the private-target copy path as a compatibility fallback.
Adds detailed logging for direct and fallback render paths, output targets, and estimated compositor resource footprints.
Adds row-level removal of stale API-layer registrations with an explicit confirmation step and an immediate post-removal refresh.
Caches Windows signature inspection until a layer DLL changes, making repeated layer-list refreshes faster.
Keeps enable, disable, reorder, and removal results synchronized with the visible registry snapshot.
Adds joystick HAT/POV directions as bindable inputs alongside buttons, with cardinal and diagonal positions.
Makes binding capture timed and cancellable, including a reliable Escape path that does not become the captured binding.
Adds conflict guidance for the new Depth Lock binding alongside existing module controls.
Captures a startup interoperability snapshot of loaded DirectX, graphics, OpenXR, and companion-layer modules plus known companion VR processes such as ReShade, DesktopXR, and SimHaptic.
Adds bounded composition-topology and downstream xrEndFrame failure logging to make multi-layer submission problems visible without flooding session logs.
Expands debug frame-pacing diagnostics with submitted display-time deltas and clearer pre-runtime xrEndFrame timing.

title: Depth tuning and diagnostics
summary: Improves Depth tuning and diagnostics for games that manage their own IPD.

items: Adds 0.1-step Convergence adjustments.
Warns when in-game Force IPD or stereo settings can override Stereo Boost.
Adds concise runtime geometry logging for troubleshooting Depth behavior.

title: Pivot & Recovery Reliability
summary: Fixes Pivot pose handling and Virtual Desktop Quadviews recovery, with safer and more flexible bindings.

items: Fixed Pivot origin capture and pose routing when applications issue VIEW-relative xrLocateViews calls.
Added non-blocking warnings when Pivot activation, Set Origin, or Release Origin share an input, including Toggle mode.
Made Virtual Desktop Quadviews recovery wait for continuously stable eye tracking before rebuilding compositor targets.
Added Numpad 0-9 support for keyboard bindings.

title: Eye-Tracking Runtime Compatibility
summary: Restores eye-tracked Quadviews on affected Virtual Desktop setups and makes startup capability decisions immediately diagnosable across runtimes.

items: Fixed eye-tracked Quadviews falling back to fixed foveation when a runtime or API-layer chain cannot complete pre-instance eye-gaze extension enumeration; VectorXR now treats that result as indeterminate, requests XR_EXT_eye_gaze_interaction optimistically, and safely retries without it when rejected.

Replaced the binary eye-gaze capability check with one authoritative tri-state extension probe, preserving completed negative results, known SteamVR and PimaxXR false-negative workarounds, and the native Varjo gaze contract.

Added an info-level Quadviews eye-gaze startup summary covering probe state and failure detail, extension-request reason, instance create and retry results, final extension state, and selected tracking path.
Added regression coverage for present, absent, and indeterminate gaze probes, including the Virtual Desktop failure mode.

title: Varjo Eye Tracking & Recovery Diagnostics
summary: Restores gaze-driven native Varjo foveation and adds targeted diagnostics for Virtual Desktop reconnect blur.

items: Fixed native Varjo Quadviews remaining fixed-center by activating foveated rendering only while the combined-eye orientation is tracked.
Added bounded, debug-only compositor resource and pixel diagnostics to identify Virtual Desktop reconnect blur without affecting normal rendering.

title: Headset Recovery & Frame Pacing
summary: Restores gaze-driven rendering after Virtual Desktop reconnects, activates native Varjo foveation when DCS omits its request, and fixes inactive-layer and Quadviews prewarm paths that could disrupt frame pacing.

items: Fixed Virtual Desktop reconnects leaving synthesized Quadviews visually stuck on a stale focus region: after a sustained eye-gaze locate failure recovers, VectorXR now rebuilds the compositor output targets so live gaze control returns without restarting the game.

Fixed native Varjo eye-tracked Quadviews when DCS enables the Varjo extension but omits its per-view foveated-rendering request; VectorXR now supplies the request while eye tracking is active, allowing the runtime to return its foveated texture sizes and moving focus geometry.

Reduced overhead when enhancements are inactive: sessions that never enable Turbo now pass frame pacing directly through, while disabled Pivot, Depth, and Quadviews paths skip unnecessary pose processing.

Fixed synthesized Quadviews output targets being prewarmed at native stereo size and rebuilt on the first composed frame at the configured focus density, removing a large first-frame stall and a runtime resource-churn path that could keep DCS below headset refresh.
Expanded Varjo foveation-request and Quadviews compositor-recovery diagnostics, with regression coverage for density scaling and runtime maximum-size clamping.

title: Pivot Reliability & Headset Compatibility
summary: Makes Pivot Always On dependable across overlapping profiles, restores eye-tracked Quadviews on affected PimaxXR setups, and expands headset diagnostics and Pivot tuning.

items: Fixed Pivot Always On profiles being discarded when their optional suspend or resume binding overlapped a higher-priority profile; automatic engagement now remains active while only the conflicting binding is shadowed.
Improved the Pivot UI, usage guide, and startup logs so Always On behavior, optional bindings, and binding-shadow warnings accurately describe what the runtime will do.
Expanded Pivot deadzone limits to 180 degrees for yaw and 90 degrees for pitch across the controls, validation, and configuration schema.

Restored eye-tracked Quadviews on PimaxXR runtimes that omit XR_EXT_eye_gaze_interaction during pre-instance enumeration but accept it when the OpenXR instance is created, retaining a safe retry for runtimes that reject it.
Added detailed native Varjo resolution and foveation contract diagnostics to distinguish application requests, runtime limits, scaling, focus movement, and headset-side caps.
Added regression coverage for PimaxXR eye-gaze compatibility and Always On profile resolution with overlapping bindings.

title: Runtime Compatibility & Sharpening
summary: Restores visible Quadviews sharpening, improves SteamVR and PSVR2 eye-tracking compatibility, and makes Turbo safer around motion smoothing and synthesized DCS quadviews.

items: Fixed Quadviews sharpening being visually cancelled at high-contrast edges, including native Varjo focus views, while avoiding redundant render-target clears to reduce composition overhead.
Improved SteamVR Quadviews compatibility by translating visibility-mask requests to stereo views and correcting reversed gaze poses from affected headset drivers.
Restored PSVR2 eye tracking through SteamVR when its pre-instance extension probe reports a false negative, with a safe retry for runtimes that truly reject the extension.
Prevented DCS with synthesized Quadviews on SteamVR from entering incompatible Turbo pacing that caused invalid display times, Waiting overlays, broken rendering, or crashes.
Made Turbo compatibility risks explicit in the app and logs, including its incompatibility with SteamVR Motion Smoothing, safer per-application guidance, and unoverrideable runtime safety blocks.
Prevented development installs from enabling duplicate VectorXR layer manifests and added bounded retries when saving runtime pacing decisions.
Added regression coverage for sharpening shaders, gaze-extension policy, and Turbo compatibility rules.

title: Performance & Runtime Hardening
summary: Refines Turbo and the core OpenXR architecture for smoother performance, broader runtime compatibility, and a clearer configuration experience.

items: Refactored Turbo frame pacing to reduce overhead, improve lifecycle stability, and avoid unnecessary performance penalties in titles that do not benefit from it.
Strengthened session, swapchain, graphics-state, tracking, and logging architecture throughout the OpenXR layer.
Reorganized Turbo into focused Runtime Behavior and Performance Diagnostics pages that keep everyday setup simple while preserving advanced controls.
Improved Quadviews compatibility and rendering resilience, including stronger native Varjo behavior and new opinionated performance presets.

title: Pivot Pitch Fix
summary: Pivot's extra pitch now rotates around your own view axis, fixing inverted or rolled pitch response for cockpits facing away from the headset's calibrated forward.

items: Fixed Pivot pitch rotating around the playspace axis instead of your current view heading - pitch pivot felt inverted or rolled sideways when your seat faced away from the headset's room-calibration forward, while yaw was unaffected.

title: Turbo Metrics
summary: Measure what Turbo actually does to your frame pacing - fps, frame times, and pacing wait time recorded per strategy and compared in the Turbo panel - plus Turbo engagement fixes validated on MSFS 2024.

items: Split turbo into two distinct strategies: async (the original Turbo) and sequenced (a new strategy for runtimes that cannot tolerate async).
Fixed a game freeze when switching to VR mode in MSFS 2024 while Turbo was available (frame-call ordering during Turbo engagement).
Turbo now waits at least 5 seconds after a session starts before engaging, so it never kicks in mid VR-mode transition.
Turbo panel now explains that Sequenced-pacing runtimes (Pimax, Oculus, Varjo) cannot exceed a runtime-enforced framerate lock.
Turbo Metrics: avg fps, 1% low, avg/p99 frame times, and runtime pacing wait time are recorded separately for Turbo off, async, and sequenced, with a per-session comparison in the Turbo panel.
Metrics collection is configurable: always-on, off, or gated behind a new capture keybinding (with its own sound cues) so loading screens and menus stay out of your data.
Sharper diagnostics: runtime submit failures, shouldRender changes, and empty-frame transitions are now logged, making black-screen reports self-explanatory.

title: Turbo Pacing Auto-Discovery
summary: Turbo now adapts its frame-pacing strategy to each headset runtime automatically, fixing the immediate self-suspension seen on Quest, Varjo, and Pimax headsets while leaving the already-working SteamVR behavior untouched. Toggling Turbo mid-flight is now instant, loading screens no longer confuse it, and a new Frame Pacing panel shows exactly what was chosen for each runtime.

items: Turbo now chooses the right frame-pacing strategy per headset runtime. Auto mode starts from what is known about your runtime, verifies it against live frame timing, adapts if needed, and remembers the verdict so the right strategy applies from the first frame of your next session.

New Sequenced pacing strategy makes Turbo work on runtimes that could not be pipelined before, including Quest and other Oculus-runtime headsets, Varjo, and Pimax. The 0.12.0 behavior of Turbo activating briefly and then suspending itself on these headsets is fixed.
Turbo now waits for the game to reach a steady frame rate before engaging and rides through loading screens, removing startup hiccups and false self-suspensions during mission loads.
The Turbo toggle binding now switches instantly, with no re-synchronization hitch, making in-flight A/B comparisons seamless.
Fixed rare full-game freezes with Turbo active, caused by a deadlock between frame pacing and pose queries inside the layer.

The Turbo page gained a Frame Pacing panel listing each runtime you have used, the strategy in effect, and how it was chosen. You can pin a strategy per runtime or clear a recorded verdict to re-discover, and the list updates live while a game is running.
Turbo and Depth toggle bindings are now compact one-line rows with a dedicated edit page, matching the Pivot layout and freeing up screen space.
Added a conflict warning on the Turbo and OpenXR Layers pages when OpenXR Toolkit is enabled alongside VectorXR Turbo, since two frame-pacing layers fight each other.
Fixed a scrambled, mismatched per-eye image that could appear when Turbo ran together with Quadviews.
Debug reports now include the per-runtime pacing history, and debug-level logs carry detailed pacing forensics to make headset-specific reports precise.

title: Turbo Mode & Pivot 2.0
summary: A major update introducing Turbo mode for systems whose fps is held back by headset frame pacing, and a greatly expanded Pivot with multiple profiles per game, custom origin points, stepped and always-on modes, and per-direction tuning, alongside a sharper Varjo focus image and refined controls throughout the app.

items: New Turbo enhancement: it frees your game from the headset runtime's frame pacing to lift performance on systems where the runtime caps fps below what your hardware can deliver. Turn it on globally or per game, with an optional in-game toggle binding for instant A/B comparisons.

Turbo protects itself automatically: on runtimes that cannot be safely pipelined (such as Pimax's PiOpenXR) it detects the resulting stalls and suspends itself instead of stuttering. Press the toggle binding to re-arm it if you want to try again.

Pivot now supports several profiles per game, arranged in priority order. Each profile has its own activation binding, so the button you press decides which rotation behavior engages, and you can switch between them live in flight.

Added optional Set Origin and Release Origin bindings so Pivot can rotate around a point you choose. Bind Set Origin to the same button as your in-game recenter and the two stay aligned; Release Origin returns to the default headset origin. Each has its own audio cue.

Added a Stepped response mode, inspired by XRNeckSafer, that adds rotation in fixed increments as your head passes configurable thresholds, with hysteresis so the view does not oscillate at a boundary.
Added an Always On activation mode that keeps Pivot engaged automatically, plus an Advanced Axes option to tune left, right, up, and down independently.
Sharpened the Varjo focus image further by widening the sharpening sample area in the native Varjo view path.

Reworked the Pivot interface: bindings and rotation settings now open on their own focused sub-pages so each profile card stays compact, disabled profiles are clearly greyed out, and turning a default profile off explains exactly what that means for your games.
The Save button now lists the settings blocking a save when it is disabled, and fields with out-of-range values are outlined in red so they are easy to find.
Added frame-pacing telemetry and expanded Pivot, origin, stepped-mode, and Turbo logging in debug exports so playback and performance issues can be diagnosed precisely.

title: Varjo Compatible Quadviews
summary: Adds a Varjo compatible quadviews mode that forwards the four native view layers to Varjo runtimes so the high-density focus panels are driven directly, replacing the stereo-composite emulation that softened the image on Varjo headsets.

items: On Varjo runtimes with native quad-view support, Quadviews now hands the four view layers (two peripheral, two focus) straight to the runtime so the physical focus panels render at full resolution instead of being flattened into a single stereo image.

Focus Scale, Peripheral Scale, and Focus Sharpness still apply (sharpening runs as a focus post-process); focus size, transition, offsets, and gaze smoothing are owned by the Varjo runtime in this mode.
Automatic on supported Varjo headsets when Quadviews is enabled, and a no-op on all other headsets, which keep the existing composite emulation.
Added a new registry-based detection mechanism for binding the correct runtime.
Pivot continues to work alongside the forwarded native views.
Added a Varjo Compatibility note in the Quadviews tab describing which controls apply.

title: Quadviews Focus & Sharpness Improvements
summary: Delivers the Quadviews focus region at full resolution end-to-end for a noticeably sharper image, turns on focus sharpening by default, retunes the default Quadviews profile, and adds deeper debug logging for focus resolution and eye tracking.

items: Fixed the Quadviews focus region being downscaled during compositing. The high-resolution focus view is now delivered at full 1:1 resolution, restoring sharpness that was previously lost and making the Focus Scale setting effective.
Dev Note: You may need to retune your Quadviews settings following this update. Previously, the Foveated Resolution setting was capped at 100%. Values above 100% will now apply correctly!

Focus sharpening now works correctly and is enabled by default, with edge clamping to avoid halos on high-contrast detail such as cockpit text and instruments. Further changes may be made here based on user feedback.
Retuned the default Quadviews profile with a larger focus region and lighter peripheral resolution for a sharper, more forgiving image out of the box at roughly a third of full-stereo pixel cost.

Added detailed Quadviews debug logging, including a focus sampling ratio and canvas density to confirm 1:1 focus rendering, plus eye-tracking interaction-profile diagnostics to help pinpoint why gaze-driven focus may be unavailable.
Added a subtle update indicator next to the version number that appears when a newer release is available on GitHub, linking to the About page for details.

title: Varjo and Pivot diagnostics
summary: Improves Quadviews compatibility and troubleshooting with stronger Varjo/OpenXR contract handling, more reliable live config reloads, safer eye-gaze fallback behavior, and detailed Pivot debug diagnostics.

items: Hardened Varjo Quadviews emulation and OpenXR next-chain handling, including COMBINED_EYE_VARJO reference-space behavior and xrGetReferenceSpaceBoundsRect support.
Improved eye-gaze setup and fallback behavior so Quadviews can continue with head/static focus when eye tracking resources are unavailable.
Improved config file watching and reload behavior so profile changes are picked up more reliably during active sessions.
Added debug-level Pivot diagnostics for tracking freshness, location flags, recomposition mode, eye offsets, and left/right pose deltas to help diagnose pivot drift or asymmetry.

title: Varjo Quadviews fix
summary: Fixes a black-screen issue with Quadviews on Varjo headsets

items: Fixed a black screen on Varjo headsets when using VectorXR Quadviews; the focus and peripheral views are now composited correctly.
Each session log now records the VectorXR layer version to make troubleshooting easier.

title: Layer startup diagnostics
summary: Adds detailed runtime logging across the OpenXR layer chain during session startup to help diagnose headset- and runtime-specific issues, with no change to runtime behavior.

items: Logs the active OpenXR runtime, headset/system details, and the application’s enabled extensions at startup.
Traces each key OpenXR call during session bring-up (session creation, reference spaces, swapchain format and creation, action-set attach, and session begin) with parameters and results.
Surfaces previously-silent downstream failures in that startup window so the exact failing call is captured in logs and debug exports.

title: Beta Release
summary: VectorXR enters beta with smoother Pivot easing, clearer and more honest Depth and Pivot controls, a color-coded Quadviews performance budget, optional sound cues for bindings, and headset runtime-compatibility guidance.

items: Pivot now eases smoothly in and out when toggled instead of snapping, with a tunable activation ramp and a single smoothing control shared by yaw and pitch.
Synchronized the Pivot yaw and pitch defaults for a consistent out-of-the-box feel.
Reworked the Depth controls with bipolar sliders centered at neutral and one value per effect, and fixed the runtime toggle to apply saved values instantly as a clean on/off switch.
Added a Depth troubleshooting notice for game or runtime settings that can override OpenXR stereo geometry.
Quadviews now color-codes its performance budget (green/amber/red) and takes Foveate/Peripheral resolution as a percent of headset resolution.
Added optional sound feedback for keybind and device bindings: play a short .wav on activate/deactivate using the bundled tones or your own, with a master volume control in Settings.
Enhancement default profiles now ship off for consistency.

title: Profile opt-in controls
summary: Per-application profiles can now opt apps into Depth, Pivot, or Quadviews even when the default profile is off, with a clearer dashboard and restored About tab for release information.

items: Changed profile resolution so the first enabled custom profile targeting an app turns that Enhancement on and applies its settings, even if the default profile is disabled.
Retired the old per-profile disable mode from the app model and profile editor; profile participation is now controlled by a simple Profile On/Off toggle.
Updated validation and runtime tests for the new custom-profile opt-in behavior.
Added an active Enhancement overview to Home with quick navigation into Quadviews, Pivot, and Depth settings.
Restored the About tab as the home for project links, Ko-fi support, update checks, and full patch notes.
Moved discovered-app tracking controls into Settings and made the Application Registry focus on unregistered apps first, with details available in a modal.

title: UI overhaul
summary: A refreshed app shell that separates a welcome dashboard from settings, sharpens the OpenXR layer manager, and unifies the Quadviews profile editors around the new "Enhancement" language.

items: Split the old Home tab into a Home dashboard (welcome, system health, patch notes, updates, and support) and a dedicated Settings tab, with Home as the default landing tab.
Folded the former About tab into Home and rewrote the welcome hero to cover foveated rendering, head rotation, and stereo depth.
Adopted "Enhancement" wording throughout the app for the OpenXR modifications.
Made OpenXR layer enabled and disabled states far more distinct with solid, high-contrast status pills in both light and dark themes.
Unified the Quadviews default and per-application profile editors on one shared layout and fixed field alignment in the Resolution group.
Replaced the sidebar VXR text mark with the app logo and evened out the Pivot binding dropdown heights.

title: Experimental Quadviews
summary: VectorXR now includes experimental native Quadviews support for OpenXR apps, with per-application profiles and compatibility with Depth and Pivot.

items: Added an experimental Quadviews module for foveal and peripheral rendering control.
Added Quadviews defaults and per-application profiles for tracking mode, focus size, resolution scale, offsets, smoothing, and transition tuning.
Added native Quadviews composition support that works alongside VectorXR Depth and Pivot.
Improved Pivot compatibility for VectorXR-managed quadview sessions, including close cockpit/HMD geometry in supported apps.
Added Quadviews diagnostics and development notes for performance tuning and future dynamic foveation work.

title: UI polish
summary: VectorXR now has cleaner About and Health Check layouts with more consistent spacing and clearer support visibility.

items: Made the Ko-fi support link more visible and moved it alongside the app description.
Aligned the About tab cards so the page spacing reads more cleanly.
Improved Health Check card alignment, status chip sizing, and footer composition.

title: Release readiness
summary: VectorXR now has in-app update checks, GitHub release automation, MIT licensing, and refreshed project documentation.

items: Added an About tab update checker that can detect newer published GitHub releases.
Added a tag-driven GitHub Actions release workflow for building Windows installers.
Added version/tag validation so release tags match the app version before a release build runs.
Added MIT licensing and clearer branding language for DienerTech LLC.
Refreshed the README with feature screenshots, installation guidance, acknowledgments, and release documentation.
Improved the About tab layout with integrated release status, patch notes, and support information.

title: OpenXR layer manager
summary: VectorXR can now inspect and manage implicit OpenXR API layers from inside the app.

items: Added an OpenXR Layers tab with registry-slice sub-tabs for machine-wide and per-user 64-bit and 32-bit implicit API layers.
Added layer enable/disable controls, adjacent move up/down ordering, and details for manifest paths, DLL paths, and Windows signature status.
Added on-demand elevation for machine-wide OpenXR layer changes instead of requiring VectorXR to always run as administrator.
Added VectorXR and Quad-Views-Foveated guidance so Pivot users can see when layer ordering may break quadviews compatibility.
Added a read-only Home status for the VectorXR OpenXR layer so users can tell whether OpenXR Enhancements  can apply at runtime.

title: Launch prep and icon pipeline cleanup
summary: VectorXR now has improved binding management and an improved icon!

items: Improved the device binding UI to better handle disconected devices.
Added a note regarding Pivot compatibility with quadviews supplied directly by the runtime, such as Pimax Play.
Replaced the ad hoc Tauri icon-generation flow with a repo-local PowerShell script for predictable `icon.png` and multi-size `icon.ico` output.
Updated the app icon assets to the latest VectorXR branding pass for continued launch evaluation.

title: Windows installer milestone
summary: VectorXR now has a local production build that creates a Windows installer with OpenXR layer registration and cleanup.

items: Added a local installer build command that builds the OpenXR layer, stages the payload, and runs the Tauri NSIS bundle.
Packaged the VectorXR OpenXR layer DLL and manifest with the desktop app installer.
Added elevated per-machine installer hooks that register the layer under the HKLM OpenXR implicit API layer registry location.
Added uninstall hooks that remove the installed VectorXR OpenXR layer registry entry.
Validated install, launch, desktop icon, registry registration, and uninstall cleanup locally.

title: Application discovery and portable profiles
summary: VectorXR can now remember OpenXR apps it has seen and turn them into profile targets when you are ready.

items: Added local OpenXR application discovery with a registry toggle and clear action.
Added an Application Registry discovery panel with refresh, launch counts, first seen, and last seen details.
Added one-click registration for discovered executables.
Migrated imported profile executable matches into registered applications so shared configs can link Depth and Pivot profiles automatically.
Simplified registered app cards with inline title editing, executable guidance, and a two-column layout on wide screens.

title: Phase 3 shell foundation
summary: The app now has a cleaner home surface, theme support, and a built-in patch notes view.

items: Renamed front-end module labels to Home, Depth, and Pivot.
Added system, light, and dark theme preferences.
Moved release notes into an in-app log so recent updates stay easy to find.

title: VectorXR suite shell
